lead: A lattice is an ordered set where every two elements have a least upper bound (join) and a greatest lower bound (meet). Order gives one definition; two operations with four laws give another, describing the same object. Lattices underlie Boolean algebra, set families closed under union and intersection, and divisibility. Circuit minimisation and query planners use join and meet.
prereq: You need Unit 2: partial orders, posets and Hasse diagrams — reflexivity, antisymmetry, transitivity, comparability.

sections.h3: Bounds of a pair, and the poset definition

blocks.text: In a poset (L, ≤), an upper bound of a, b is any u with a ≤ u and b ≤ u. A lower bound is any l with l ≤ a and l ≤ b. Bounds may be missing or many.
The least upper bound is the upper bound below every other. The greatest lower bound is the lower bound above every other. Antisymmetry makes each unique when it exists.
a ∨ b = lub{a, b},   a ∧ b = glb{a, b}
blocks.where: a ∨ b is the join of a and b, also written sup(a, b); a ∧ b is the meet, also written inf(a, b). Read ∨ as join and ∧ as meet. In a Boolean lattice they behave like OR and AND, but here they are order concepts.

blocks.text: (L, ≤) is a lattice when every pair a, b has join and meet in L. Pairs suffice: by induction every nonempty finite subset has both. Infinite subsets may fail; the rationals have no least upper bound for numbers whose square is below 2.

sections.h3: Four small posets put to the test

blocks.text: Comparable pairs are easy: if a ≤ b then a ∨ b = b and a ∧ b = a. Trouble comes from incomparable pairs.

items: Chain: positive integers under ≤; join=max, meet=min. Every chain is a lattice.
Diamond: {1, 2, 3, 6} under divisibility; 2, 3 incomparable, upper bound 6 only, lower 1 only, so 2 ∨ 3 = 6 and 2 ∧ 3 = 1. Lattice.
Divisors of 12: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}; join = lcm, meet = gcd, both stay in A.

Failure: B = {2, 3, 6, 12}. Upper bounds of 2 and 3 are 6 and 12; 6 divides 12, so 2 ∨ 3 = 6 exists. But 2 and 3 have no common lower bound in B because 1 is not in B, so 2 ∧ 3 does not exist. Thus B is not a lattice. For a missing join use {2, 3, 12, 18}: upper bounds of 2, 3 are 12 and 18, neither divides the other, so 2 ∨ 3 does not exist.

blocks.text: An algebraic lattice is a set L with binary ∨, ∧ such that for all a, b, c:

items: Idempotent: a ∨ a = a and a ∧ a = a.
Commutative: a ∨ b = b ∨ a and a ∧ b = b ∧ a.
Associative: (a ∨ b) ∨ c = a ∨ (b ∨ c), and the same with ∧.
Absorption: a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a and a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a.

blocks.text: No order, bottom or top is assumed. The views are equivalent. A poset lattice satisfies the laws. Conversely, define a ≤ b to mean a ∧ b = a.

items: Antisymmetric: if a ∧ b = a and b ∧ a = b, then a = a ∧ b = b ∧ a = b.
Transitive: if a ∧ b = a and b ∧ c = b, then a ∧ c = (a ∧ b) ∧ c = a ∧ (b ∧ c) = a ∧ b = a.
Lower bound: (a ∧ b) ∧ a = a ∧ b, so a ∧ b ≤ a; similarly ≤ b. Greatest: if x ≤ a, b then x ∧ (a ∧ b) = (x ∧ a) ∧ b = x ∧ b = x, so x ≤ a ∧ b.
Upper bound: a ≤ a ∨ b is absorption a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a; the other law gives b ≤ a ∨ b. Least: if a ≤ x, b ≤ x then (a ∨ b) ∨ x = a ∨ (b ∨ x) = a ∨ x = x, so a ∨ b ≤ x.

blocks.text: Thus a ∧ b is glb and a ∨ b is lub. Duality: swap ∨ with ∧ and reverse ≤; true statements stay true. Some syllabi call these the poset and algebraic versions.

figure.caption: The divisors of 12 ordered by divisibility, with 1 at the bottom and 12 at the top. Notice that 2 and 3 are incomparable, with join 6 and meet 1.

spec.aria: Hasse diagram of the divisors of 12 ordered by divisibility, with 1 at the bottom and 12 at the top.

examples.question: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12} be ordered by divisibility, so a ≤ b means a divides b. (a) Find 4 ∨ 6 and 4 ∧ 6. (b) Find 2 ∨ 3 and 2 ∧ 3. (c) Find 3 ∨ 4 and 3 ∧ 4. (d) Decide whether A is a lattice. (5 marks)
steps: a ≤ b when b = k·a. The covers are the edges of the figure.
For 4, 6: common multiples in A: 12 only, so join 12. Common divisors: 1, 2; greatest 2, so meet 2.
For 2, 3: upper bounds 6, 12; 6 divides 12, so join 6. Lower bound only 1, so meet 1.
For 3, 4: lcm 12, gcd 1, so join 12, meet 1.
The incomparable pairs are {2, 3}, {3, 4}, {4, 6}; each has join and meet in A. Comparable pairs are automatic. So A is a lattice.
Under divisibility join = lcm and meet = gcd; both stay inside A for all 36 ordered pairs (a, b), that is, for every choice of a and b in A.

traps: Naming any upper bound the least upper bound. In {2, 3, 12, 18} under divisibility, 12 and 18 are both upper bounds of 2 and 3, and neither divides the other, so 2 and 3 have no least upper bound.
Checking only comparable pairs. Those always give join=larger, meet=smaller; marks lie in incomparable pairs.
Swapping join and meet. Join is upper (lcm under divisibility), meet lower (gcd).
Believing a lattice needs bottom and top. Only pairs need bounds; positive integers under ≤ form a lattice with no top.
Confusing lattice with Hasse diagram. Diagram is a picture; lattice is set with order.

quiz.q: Define the join and the meet of two elements of a poset.
quiz.a: a ∨ b is lub{a, b}; a ∧ b is glb{a, b}. Each is unique when it exists.

quiz.q: State the four pairs of laws of an algebraic lattice.
quiz.a: Idempotent: a ∨ a = a, a ∧ a = a. Commutative for both. Associative for both. Absorption: a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a and a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a.

quiz.q: Why can a pair in a poset have at most one least upper bound?
quiz.a: Two least upper bounds u and v would each be ≤ the other, since each is an upper bound and the other is least. Antisymmetry gives u = v.

quiz.q: State the principle of duality for lattices and give the dual of a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a.
quiz.a: Interchange ∨ with ∧ and reverse ≤; true statements stay true. The dual of a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a is a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a.

quiz.q: In the poset of divisors of 30 under divisibility, find 6 ∨ 10 and 6 ∧ 10 and say whether they lie in the set.
quiz.a: lcm(6, 10) = 30 and gcd(6, 10) = 2. Both are divisors of 30, so 6 ∨ 10 = 30 and 6 ∧ 10 = 2, both inside the set.

quiz.q: In A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12} under divisibility, find 2 ∨ 4 and 2 ∧ 4, and 4 ∨ 6 and 4 ∧ 6.
quiz.a: 2 divides 4, so 2 ∨ 4 = 4 and 2 ∧ 4 = 2. For 4 and 6 the only common multiple in A is 12 and gcd is 2, so 4 ∨ 6 = 12 and 4 ∧ 6 = 2.

quiz.q: Show that B = {2, 3, 6, 12} under divisibility is not a lattice.
quiz.a: Upper bounds of 2 and 3 in B are 6 and 12; 6 divides 12, so 2 ∨ 3 = 6 exists. 2 and 3 have no lower bound in B because 1 is not in B, so 2 ∧ 3 does not exist. One missing meet suffices. (Or B = {2, 3, 12, 18} has missing join.)

quiz.q: Starting from the four laws, prove that the relation a ≤ b defined by a ∧ b = a is transitive, and that a ∧ b is a lower bound of a.
quiz.a: Assume a ∧ b = a and b ∧ c = b. Then a ∧ c = (a ∧ b) ∧ c = a ∧ (b ∧ c) = a ∧ b = a, so a ≤ c. Also (a ∧ b) ∧ a = (b ∧ a) ∧ a = b ∧ (a ∧ a) = b ∧ a = a ∧ b, so a ∧ b ≤ a.

beyond: Not for the exam. Lattice theory underlies formal concept analysis and closed itemset mining. Compilers use subtyping lattices; static analysers use complete lattices of program states in abstract interpretation. Every finite distributive lattice is isomorphic to a family of sets closed under union and intersection — Birkhoff's representation theorem. Search: complete lattice, formal concept analysis, Birkhoff representation theorem, abstract interpretation.
